location: Task 2 Step 3, AllocationService.release (plan lines 583-618): `const allocations = await tx.orderLineAllocation.findMany({ where: { orderLine: { orderId } } ... })` is a plain, unlocked read, followed by relative `increment` updates and `deleteMany`.
title: Two concurrent release() calls on the same order both restore the stock, creating stock that does not exist, and the ledger agrees with the cache
failure_scenario: Batch X: received 500. Order O1 is confirmed for 200 and O2 for 200, so X has 100 left. The admin double-clicks Cancel on O1, or cancels it from two tabs, so two transactions call release(O1). Under READ COMMITTED both findMany calls see O1's allocation of 200. Tx A runs `increment 200`, which brings X to 300, writes ORDER_OUT +200, deletes the allocation and commits. Tx B's UPDATE was waiting on the row lock; it now applies to the new row version (300 + 200 = 500). That passes `qtyUnitsRemaining BETWEEN 0 AND qtyUnitsReceived` because 500 <= 500. B writes a second ORDER_OUT +200, and its `deleteMany` quietly removes 0 rows. The result: the warehouse shows 500 while only 300 are physically there (O2's 200 are still allocated). The ledger is 500-200-200+200+200 = 500, which equals the cache, so ledger-assert stays silent. The CHECK only masks this when the batch had no other consumers, which is the only case the plan's test ('release restores the batch', a single order on a fresh batch) covers. Task 7 only avoids it if it happens to use a conditional status update, and the plan does not say so. Rule 1 says locking belongs in this service.
fix:
Make release self-protecting by locking the allocation rows before reading them. A second caller then blocks, re-checks after the first commits, sees the rows are deleted and does nothing:
```ts
const allocations = await tx.$queryRaw<{ id: string; batchId: string; qtyUnits: number; itemId: string }[]>`
  SELECT a.id, a."batchId", a."qtyUnits", l."itemId"
  FROM "order_line_allocations" a
  JOIN "order_lines" l ON l.id = a."orderLineId"
  WHERE l."orderId" = ${orderId}
  ORDER BY a."batchId", a.id
  FOR UPDATE OF a`;
```
Then lock the batches in the same canonical order that allocate uses (see the deadlock finding) before incrementing. Add a concurrent test: seed X with 5 boxes, confirm O1 for 200 and O2 for 200, run `Promise.allSettled([releaseInTx(O1), releaseInTx(O2 is NOT released) ...])`, that is `Promise.allSettled([releaseInTx(o1), releaseInTx(o1)])`, then assert X.qtyUnitsRemaining === 300 and that ORDER_OUT for refId o1 sums to 0. O2 must exist so the batch CHECK cannot hide the bug.

location: Task 2 'Produces' plus Step 3 allocate signature `opts: { orderId: string; actorUserId: string }` (plan lines 321-324, 501-505). Header rules 1 and 3 (lines 25-27).
title: allocate() never locks or checks the order, so confirming the same order twice at once allocates it twice with no error
failure_scenario: The admin double-clicks Confirm on order O (qty 200) and the batch holds 500. Both requests read O as PLACED (Task 5 as summarised has no lock), and both call allocate(tx, [{itemId, 200}], {orderId: O}). FOR UPDATE on the batches only serialises them, and there is enough stock, so both succeed. The batch drops to 100, there are two sets of ORDER_OUT(-200, refId O) and two sets of allocation rows, and status is set to CONFIRMED twice. At delivery (Task 6 credits 'every allocation on the order') the client receives 400. Cache and ledger agree, so ledger-assert is silent. Task 5's planned 'confirming twice is refused' test is sequential and passes anyway. The plan's only concurrency test covers two different orders on one batch, never the same order twice.

location: Task 2 'Produces' (lines 321-324) and Step 3: allocate returns `AllocationResult[]` keyed only by itemId and writes no OrderLineAllocation rows. release (lines 588-617) reads OrderLineAllocation rows. Task 5 (line 680) is expected to 'write OrderLineAllocation rows, set qtyUnitsFulfilled'.
title: What allocate takes out and what release puts back come from two different sources, joined only by caller code in Task 5
failure_scenario: Warehouse stock leaves in AllocationService but is recorded, and later restored, from rows that OrdersService writes. Any mismatch in Task 5 silently breaks the zero-sum. Examples: (1) it writes allocation rows with qtyUnitsRequested instead of result.qtyUnitsAllocated on a short line; (2) it maps results back by `itemId`, and order_lines has no @@unique([orderId, itemId]), so two lines for one item both take the first result; (3) it writes rows only for fully fulfilled lines. Afterwards, release restores more or less than was taken, and delivery credits the client for goods that never shipped. Every restore writes a matching movement, so cache and ledger agree. It also makes the Task 2 test `confirmAnOrderFor` impossible to write without copying Task 5's persistence logic into the test, so the release test exercises test code rather than the product path.
fix: Have allocate write its own record. Change to `interface AllocationRequest { orderLineId: string; itemId: string; qtyUnits: number }`, and in the batch loop do `await tx.orderLineAllocation.create({ data: { orderLineId: request.orderLineId, batchId: batch.id, qtyUnits: take } })`. After the loop do `await tx.orderLine.update({ where: { id: request.orderLineId }, data: { qtyUnitsFulfilled: request.qtyUnits - outstanding } })`. Return results keyed by orderLineId. Add `@@unique([orderId, itemId])` to OrderLine in Task 1. Task 5 then only recomputes totals and status.

location: Task 2 Step 1, tests 'allocates the earliest-expiring batch first' (`seedBatch({ batchNumber: 'EARLY', expiryDays: 30, ... })`, line 333) and 'spans batches when one is not enough' (line 343). The query `AND "expiryDate" > ${cutoff}` is at line 524.
title: Tests 1 and 2 put EARLY exactly on the 30-day default, so the strict '>' drops it and Step 4 cannot pass. The easy fixes are wrong.
failure_scenario: The default for expiry.minShelfLifeOnDeliveryDays is 30 (setting-defaults.ts line 16). @prisma/adapter-pg sends the Date param untyped as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm' UTC (formatDateTime in adapter-pg dist/index.js lines 389-393). Postgres infers `date` from `"expiryDate" > $n`, so the cutoff becomes UTC-date(now+30d). A batch seeded at expiryDays 30 is stored as that same UTC date (formatDate for DATE columns), and `d > d` is false, so EARLY is always excluded. Test 1 then gets allocated[0] = LATE and fails. Test 2 gets [{LATE, 350}] and fails. This happens at any time of day. An implementer told to make it pass will likely change `>` to `>=` or loosen the cutoff. That silently changes the spec's §7.3 rule (`expiryDate > today + minShelfLife`) and nothing else in the suite would notice.
fix: Change the test data, not the query. Use `expiryDays: 60` for EARLY in tests 1 and 2 (LATE stays at 300). Add explicit boundary tests pinned to the spec: `seedBatch({batchNumber:'EDGE', expiryDays: 30})` must NOT be allocated, and `seedBatch({batchNumber:'JUST_OK', expiryDays: 31})` must be. Build seedBatch expiries as a UTC calendar date (see the helpers finding) so the boundary is deterministic.

location: Task 2 Step 1 (lines 326-452): uses `seedBatch`, `allocateInTx`, `batchIdOf`, `confirmAnOrderFor`, `releaseInTx`, `itemId`, `prisma`, `AllocationResult` but never defines them. There is also no describe block, setup, or imports.
title: The test helpers are never defined, and the obvious ways to write them make key tests pass without testing anything
failure_scenario: (a) If seedBatch creates only the WarehouseBatch (for example `prisma.warehouseBatch.create`), there is no PURCHASE_IN movement. 'the ledger still sums to the cache' then compares -200 with 300 and fails, and someone may 'fix' it by narrowing the ledger filter. (b) If allocateInTx shares one tx client between the two concurrent calls, Prisma runs their queries in sequence on one connection, the FOR UPDATE never blocks itself, and the second decrement hits the CHECK. The whole transaction rolls back and both calls reject, yet every assertion (remaining >= 0, |sum| <= 300, sum of fulfilled <= 300) still passes. (c) confirmAnOrderFor needs a real users row, an orders row (totalAmount is NOT NULL) and an order_lines row with every snapshot column, and it must write the allocation rows itself. Written carelessly, release finds nothing and the test fails for the wrong reason. (d) No settings reset exists, so a stored `expiry.minShelfLifeOnDeliveryDays` left by another suite changes the results.

location: Task 1 as a whole, Step 4 (line 303). The plan never mentions the per-file cleanup chains in backend/test (for example search-normalisation.spec.ts lines 104-116 and 183-212, batches.e2e-spec.ts 52-58/75-80, items/categories/search e2e, and user-only chains in auth-login, auth-register, auth-guards, auth-throttle, media, admin-users).
title: The new FK tables break every existing suite's deleteMany cleanup, including the CHECK block that Step 4 extends
failure_scenario: Prisma creates required relations without onDelete as ON DELETE RESTRICT: cart_lines.itemId, order_lines.itemId, client_inventory_items.itemId, order_line_allocations.batchId, client_batch_holdings.batchId and orders.clientId. Step 4's 'qtyUnitsFulfilled above requested rejected' test must first insert a valid orders row. The next beforeEach in that block runs `prisma.user.deleteMany()`, which fails on orders_clientId_fkey, and every later test in the block plus its afterAll fails. Once the allocation spec or the Task 3-7 e2e files leave any row behind, `warehouseBatch.deleteMany()` and `item.deleteMany()` throw FK errors in other files. With fileParallelism:false and no fixed file order, this gives 'passes alone, fails in the full run'. There is also a Phase 2 trap that Phase 3 makes live: stock_movements.clientId is ON DELETE SET NULL, but CHECK stock_movements_owner_consistent forbids CLIENT with a NULL clientId. So after Task 6 writes DELIVERY_IN rows, the auth-* files' `user.deleteMany()` (which never clears stock_movements) fails with 23514.

location: Task 1 Step 3 hand-written SQL, `orders_cancel_disposition_required CHECK ("status" <> 'CANCELLED' OR "cancelDisposition" IS NOT NULL)` (lines 290-296), with the comment 'A cancelled order that was ever allocated must say where the goods went' and line 299 'the database's copy of the §7.4 rule'.
title: The disposition CHECK contradicts Task 7 and its own comment, and does not enforce the §7.4 rule it claims to copy
failure_scenario: (1) The SQL requires a disposition on every cancelled order, including never-allocated PLACED ones. Task 7's CANCELLATION_RULES says `dispositionRequired: false` for PLACED and CONFIRMED, and the client endpoint takes no disposition, so a literal implementation fails every client cancel and every CONFIRMED cancel with a 23514 error, which surfaces as a 500. (2) The natural patch, `cancelDisposition: dto.disposition ?? 'NOT_ALLOCATED'`, passes this CHECK. But it also lets an OUT_FOR_DELIVERY or CONFIRMED order be cancelled as NOT_ALLOCATED, or a CONFIRMED order as WRITTEN_OFF, with no release. The allocated stock then stays out of the warehouse for good while the ledger and cache agree, which is the exact silent loss §7.4 exists to prevent. The CHECK cannot tell those cases apart because it ignores confirmedAt and dispatchedAt.
fix:
Tie the disposition to lifecycle timestamps the schema already has:
```sql
ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "orders_cancel_disposition_consistent" CHECK (
     ("status" <> 'CANCELLED' AND "cancelDisposition" IS NULL)
  OR ("status" = 'CANCELLED' AND "confirmedAt" IS NULL  AND "cancelDisposition" = 'NOT_ALLOCATED')
  OR ("status" = 'CANCELLED' AND "confirmedAt" IS NOT NULL AND "dispatchedAt" IS NULL AND "cancelDisposition" = 'RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE')
  OR ("status" = 'CANCELLED' AND "dispatchedAt" IS NOT NULL AND "cancelDisposition" IN ('RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE','WRITTEN_OFF'))
);
```
In Task 7, the server sets the disposition for PLACED (NOT_ALLOCATED) and CONFIRMED (RETURNED_TO_WAREHOUSE, or add an enum value RELEASED_BEFORE_DISPATCH). Only OUT_FOR_DELIVERY takes it from the request. Fix the comment. Step 4 tests: a PLACED cancel with WRITTEN_OFF is rejected, a CONFIRMED (not dispatched) cancel with WRITTEN_OFF is rejected, and a disposition on a non-cancelled order is rejected.

location: Task 2 Step 1 'TWO CONCURRENT allocations never oversell one batch' (lines 405-434) and Step 5 (lines 627-633). This adds to known issue (a).
title: Adds to known (a): even with the CHECK set aside, the race window depends on timing, and the correct assertion is 'both succeed, 200 + 100'
failure_scenario: Nothing forces tx B's SELECT to run while tx A holds an uncommitted decrement. B first does `settings.get`, which is a round trip on another pool connection, before its SELECT. If A has committed by then, B reads 100 and allocates 100 correctly even without FOR UPDATE. So Step 5's 'watch it fail' result depends on timing. Separately, with the CHECK in place, the observable difference FOR UPDATE makes is 'B is correctly partially filled' versus 'B throws 23514 (500)'. The plan's assertions (allSettled plus upper bounds) accept both outcomes.

location: Task 1 Step 3 (lines 263-269): `npx prisma migrate dev --name ordering && npx prisma generate`, then 'Then a hand-written migration' with no command, folder name, or apply step.
title: The plan never says how to create or apply the hand-written CHECK migration. The obvious reading edits an already-applied migration and causes the drift/reset prompt Phase 2 hit.
failure_scenario: After Step 3, `<ts>_ordering` is already applied to the dev DB (medinv). If the implementer pastes the CHECK SQL into that same migration.sql, its checksum changes. The dev DB keeps tables without CHECKs, while the test DB (migrated fresh by test/global-setup.ts `migrate deploy`) gets the edited file with CHECKs, so tests pass. The next `prisma migrate dev` reports that the migration was modified after it was applied and asks to reset the dev database. That is an interactive prompt: it hangs or wipes dev data, which is Phase 2's failure mode. If they instead hand-create a folder, they must pick a timestamp that sorts after `_ordering`. Phase 2's own plan text used `20260927000001_...`, which sorts before `20260927180743_catalog`, and the as-built had to rename it to `20260927180800_search_and_constraints`.
fix:
Spell out one atomic migration:
```bash
cd backend
npx prisma validate
npx prisma migrate dev --create-only --name ordering
# append the CHECK block to prisma/migrations/<new-ts>_ordering/migration.sql (after the CREATE TABLEs)
npx prisma migrate dev          # applies it to medinv
npx prisma generate             # Prisma 7 migrate dev does not regenerate reliably (see Phase 2 Step 4 note)
npx prisma migrate diff --from-config-datasource --to-schema prisma/schema.prisma --script
# must print: -- This is an empty migration.
```
Or follow Phase 2's as-built pattern: run `npx prisma migrate dev --create-only --name ordering_constraints` after `_ordering` is applied, which creates an empty, correctly timestamped folder, then fill it and run `npx prisma migrate dev`. Never edit a migration that has been applied. The searchText trigger has no bearing here: new tables and back-relations add no columns to items, so no drift comes from it.

location: Task 1 Step 4 (line 303): 'Add to test/integration/search-normalisation.spec.ts's constraint block: negative cart quantity rejected; qtyUnitsFulfilled above requested rejected; negative client holding rejected; CANCELLED with a null disposition rejected.'
title: The planned CHECK regression tests can pass without the CHECKs, and two of the six new constraints get no test
failure_scenario: The existing pattern is `.rejects.toThrow()` with no matcher, so any error passes. The new tables have many NOT NULL columns without DB defaults: Prisma's `@default(uuid())` and `@updatedAt` produce `"id" TEXT NOT NULL` and `"updatedAt" TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL` with no DEFAULT (see the auth_accounts migration). Postgres checks NOT NULL before CHECK. So `INSERT INTO client_inventory_items ("clientId","itemId","qtyUnits") VALUES ($1,$2,-1)` fails on updatedAt, and an order_lines insert missing lineTotal or pricePerBoxSnapshot, or with a bad FK, fails for that reason instead. Each test passes even if a later `migrate dev` dropped the CHECK, which is exactly what these tests exist to catch. The list also skips order_line_allocations_qty_positive, client_inventory_qty_non_negative, and the `qtyUnitsRequested > 0` half of order_lines_qty_sane. The ordering constraints also do not belong in the search spec.
fix: Create `backend/test/integration/ordering-constraints.spec.ts` with the same module setup (`imports: [AppConfigModule], providers: [PrismaService]`) and resetDb. For each of the six constraints: (1) a positive control that inserts a fully valid row and `.resolves.toBe(1)`; (2) the same row with one bad value, asserted by name, for example `.rejects.toThrow(/violates check constraint "client_inventory_qty_non_negative"/)`. Prisma 7 raw errors are P2010 'Raw query failed. Code: `23514`. Message: `…`' and include the constraint name. Always supply `id` (gen_random_uuid()) and `"updatedAt"` (now()) in raw inserts into carts and client_inventory_items.

location: Task 2 Step 3 comment 'ORDER BY is a deterministic TOTAL order, id included. Two transactions that lock the same rows in different orders deadlock' (lines 516-518). The per-request loop is `for (const request of requests)` and release updates batches in findMany order (lines 588-597).
title: The deadlock-freedom claim holds for one item only; confirmations with items in opposite order, or a confirm running alongside a cancel, can deadlock
failure_scenario: Order A has lines [X, Y] and order B has lines [Y, X], in cart-derived order with no ORDER BY. Tx A locks X's batches, tx B locks Y's, then each waits on the other. After deadlock_timeout (1s) Postgres aborts one with 40P01. adapter-pg maps that to TransactionWriteConflict, which Prisma raises as P2034, and the admin gets a 500. release() increments batches in arbitrary findMany order with no lock ordering, so a cancel that touches batches X1 and X2 can deadlock against a confirmation locking X1 then X2. The claim is untested, which breaks rule 3.
fix: Lock every candidate for every item in one statement with a global order: `WHERE "itemId" = ANY(${itemIds}::text[]) AND "qtyUnitsRemaining" > 0 AND "expiryDate" > ${cutoff} ORDER BY "itemId", "expiryDate", "receivedAt", id FOR UPDATE`, then group by itemId in JS and allocate each request from its group. In release, lock the batches first with `SELECT id FROM "warehouse_batches" WHERE id = ANY(${batchIds}::text[]) ORDER BY "itemId", "expiryDate", "receivedAt", id FOR UPDATE` before incrementing. Add a concurrent test with two orders whose lines are [X,Y] and [Y,X] and assert both settle fulfilled.

location: Task 2 Step 1, 'skips a batch with insufficient shelf life' (lines 355-364), the only shelf-life test, which relies on the default value. Step 3: `await this.settings.get('expiry.minShelfLifeOnDeliveryDays')` (line 506).
title: No test shows the shelf-life cutoff comes from settings, so a hardcoded 30 passes the whole suite
failure_scenario: The setting exists and is typed `number` (setting-defaults.ts line 16 plus Widen<>), so the plan's call compiles. But `const minShelfLifeDays = 30`, or the test's own literal used as a constant, passes every Task 2 test. The spec lists this as admin-editable (§9). An admin who raises it to 90 for a fragile product would see nothing change, and clinics would keep receiving 31-day stock.

location: Task 2 'Produces': '**must be called inside a transaction; it takes the transaction client as its first argument and will not open its own.**' (line 323). Signature `allocate(tx: Prisma.TransactionClient, ...)` (line 502).
title: Nothing enforces 'must be called inside a transaction': PrismaService type-checks as the tx argument
failure_scenario: `Prisma.TransactionClient` is `Omit<DefaultPrismaClient, ITXClientDenyList>`. In Prisma 7.10 the deny list is only `$connect/$disconnect/$on/$use/$extends` (runtime/client.d.ts line 467), so PrismaService is assignable and `'$transaction' in tx` cannot tell the two apart. A later caller, such as a Phase 5/6 admin 'quick allocate' or a test, can write `allocation.allocate(this.prisma, ...)`. Each statement then autocommits: FOR UPDATE locks only for that one SELECT, and when an allocation spans several batches the earlier decrements and ORDER_OUT rows commit before a later step throws. That leaves warehouse stock gone with no OrderLineAllocation rows. Cache and ledger agree, so nothing detects it.

location: Task 2 Step 3: `const minShelfLifeDays = await this.settings.get(...)` inside allocate (line 506). SettingsService.get uses `this.prisma`, not `tx` (settings.service.ts line 16).
title: allocate reads settings on a second pool connection while holding a transaction open, which can starve the pool and makes the cutoff impossible to pin in tests
failure_scenario: PrismaPg(connectionString) creates a pg Pool with the default max of 10. With 10 concurrent confirmations, each interactive transaction holds a connection and then waits for another one to read the setting. None can proceed until Prisma's 5 s interactive-transaction timeout kills them all (P2028). This is unlikely with one admin but guaranteed under load. Computing `Date.now()` inside the service also means no test can freeze the clock, which is why known issue (b) cannot be tested.
fix: Have the caller resolve the cutoff before opening the transaction, and pass it in: `opts: { orderId; actorUserId; minExpiryExclusive: string /* 'YYYY-MM-DD', computed in business.timezone */ }`. Compare it with `"expiryDate" > ${minExpiryExclusive}::date`. Alternatively, read the setting through `tx.setting.findUnique`. Either way the boundary becomes testable with a fixed date.

location: Task 1 Step 3 CHECK block (lines 271-297) and Step 1 models OrderLine / Order / HotDealEntry.
title: Cheap CHECKs are missing for invariants that would otherwise break silently: box/unit agreement, snapshot sanity, non-negative money, hot-deal kind
failure_scenario: A Task 5 admin edit updates `qtyBoxesRequested` but forgets `qtyUnitsRequested`, or the reverse. The line then bills for one quantity and allocates another, with no error. A `unitsPerBoxSnapshot` of 0 or a negative `lineTotal`/`totalAmount` from a bad calculation is stored as-is. `HotDealEntry.kind` is a free String, so 'Manual' instead of 'MANUAL' quietly drops an admin pin from the 'MANUAL sorted first' rule.
fix: Add to the same migration: `ALTER TABLE "order_lines" ADD CONSTRAINT "order_lines_units_match_boxes" CHECK ("qtyUnitsRequested" = "qtyBoxesRequested" * "unitsPerBoxSnapshot" AND "unitsPerBoxSnapshot" > 0 AND "pricePerBoxSnapshot" >= 0 AND "lineTotal" >= 0);`, `ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "orders_total_non_negative" CHECK ("totalAmount" >= 0);`, `ALTER TABLE "hot_deal_entries" ADD CONSTRAINT "hot_deal_kind_known" CHECK ("kind" IN ('FREQUENT','NEW','MANUAL'));`. Give each its own named-constraint test.

location: Header 'Consumes from Phases 0–2' table row `@Roles(Role.ADMIN)`, `@CurrentUser()`, `ClientOwnershipGuard` (line 55). The plan uses it for `GET /api/v1/orders/:id` and `POST /api/v1/orders/:id/cancel` (Tasks 4 and 7).
title: ClientOwnershipGuard treats `:id` as a client id, so it cannot protect order-id routes
failure_scenario: src/auth/guards/client-ownership.guard.ts line 31 does `const target = req.params?.clientId ?? req.params?.id; if (target && target !== user.sub) throw FORBIDDEN`. On `/orders/:id`, `:id` is an order uuid and never equals the user id, so every client gets a 403 on their own order and on their own PLACED-order cancel. If someone 'fixes' that by dropping the guard, cross-client reads open up unless the service scopes the query.
fix: State in the header that ClientOwnershipGuard applies only to routes keyed by `:clientId`. For order routes, scope in the service: `prisma.order.findFirst({ where: { id, ...(user.role === Role.CLIENT ? { clientId: user.sub } : {}) } })`, and return ORDER_NOT_FOUND (404) on a miss so order ids are not revealed. Add an e2e test in which client A reads client B's order and gets a 404.
